name: Lp(a) and Cardiovascular Disease
blurb: Heart attack, stroke, peripheral artery disease and residual risk.
title: Lp(a) and Cardiovascular Disease
answer: High Lp(a) raises the risk of coronary heart disease, heart attack, ischaemic stroke and peripheral artery disease, independently of LDL cholesterol. It is a major source of residual risk, the risk that remains after LDL is well treated.

reading.body:
High Lp(a) raises the risk of coronary heart disease, heart attack, ischaemic stroke and peripheral artery disease independently of LDL cholesterol, and it is a major source of residual risk after LDL is well treated.

The pattern in the evidence is threefold. Observational studies link higher Lp(a) levels to more cardiovascular events. Genetic studies show that people born with variants producing high Lp(a) have more heart disease, a natural experiment that avoids most confounding. And biology offers a mechanism by which the particle could damage arteries. A 2026 review of the evidence, cited here, treats Lp(a) as an established independent and genetically determined causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and aortic stenosis.

What matters for patients is that high Lp(a) does not mean a heart attack is certain. Many people with high Lp(a) never have one, particularly when other risk factors are controlled. The practical implication is to lower everything else that is modifiable, LDL, blood pressure, glucose and smoking, more aggressively.

What the data does not establish is how much Lp(a) lowering is needed to remove the excess risk, or whether every method of lowering it helps. Genetic studies suggest large absolute reductions may be required for a measurable difference, which may help explain the pelacarsen result and why trials of drugs that lower Lp(a) more deeply are watched closely.

explainer:
Three kinds of evidence point to Lp(a) as a cause of heart disease. Observational studies link higher levels to more events. Genetic studies show that people born with gene variants giving high Lp(a) have more heart disease, a natural experiment that avoids most confounding. And biology explains how the particle could damage arteries.

What is not yet established is how much lowering is needed to remove the excess risk, or whether every way of lowering it helps. Genetic studies suggest large absolute reductions may be required to make a measurable difference, which may help explain the pelacarsen result and why trials of drugs that lower Lp(a) more deeply are watched closely.
